item.title: Reducing Decoding Latency in Quantum Error Correction by Early Starting Clustering
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) grows and resolves syndrome clusters incrementally during stabilizer measurements, cutting post-measurement growth steps and outperforming batch Union-Find logical error rates when idling noise during decoding exceeds physical noise.

Grade 0.493 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Tommaso Peduzzi, Lukas Bödeker, Markus Müller, Luis Colmenarez

Figure

Logical error probability pL plotted against physical error rate p across code distances d=7,9,11 for four increasing idling-noise strengths 1/N, showing CAYG maintaining a higher effective threshold than standard Union-Find as idling noise increases.

Asks

Can quantum error correction decoding begin during syndrome extraction to reduce post-measurement latency and overall logical error rates under idling decoherence?

Before

Standard Union-Find waits for all d syndrome extraction rounds, yielding higher accuracy but larger post-measurement latency and faster threshold degradation under idling noise.

But

Phenomenological noise model with equal-strength idling decoherence, rotated surface codes only; hardware-level timing and circuit-level noise not evaluated.

Tools

Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG) decoding · Union-Find decoder · rotated surface codes · phenomenological noise model · Monte Carlo simulations

Abstract

In quantum error correction, fast low-latency decoding is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as delays in processing syndrome data can lead to the backlog problem. Existing decoders, including parallelizable approaches such as Union-Find, begin decoding only after all stabilizer measurement outcomes from an error-correction cycle have been received, inherently introducing a delay before decoding begins. We introduce Cluster-As-You-Go (CAYG), a modification of the Union-Find decoder that processes syndrome information during stabilizer measurements by clustering and correcting errors as they appear. This approach reduces the size of the remaining decoding problem at the end of the quantum error correction cycle and, consequently, the time required to complete the decoding process. While this early start of clustering incurs a modest reduction in decoding accuracy, it preserves the decoder's scalability. Surface-code simulations show that the resulting reduction in post-measurement idling can outweigh the accuracy loss, yielding an improved speed-accuracy trade-off. These results demonstrate that real-time, early-starting decoding during QEC cycles is both feasible and can be advantageous for quantum error correction. Demonstrated here for the surface code, CAYG is broadly applicable to other quantum error-correcting codes, which allow for clustering-based decoding approaches, and is extensible to dedicated real-time decoding hardware.

item.title: Quantum Codes for Generalized Amplitude-damping Noise
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) on a five-qubit permutation-invariant code achieves fidelity loss that scales quadratically with generalized amplitude-damping strength γ, O(γ2), under post-selected recovery.

Grade 0.465 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Sourav Dutta, Anubhab Rudra, Manav Seksaria, Anil Prabhakar, Prabha Mandayam

Figure

Entanglement fidelity and recovery probability as functions of damping strength γ at excitation parameter p=0.05. The numerically optimized code achieves higher entanglement fidelity than the [5,1] permutation-invariant code at the cost of lower success probability.

Asks

Can probabilistic and approximate quantum error correction frameworks be combined to suppress first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors in short codes?

Before

Deterministic quantum codes (such as the [5,1,3] stabilizer code) cannot eliminate first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors and incur fidelity loss scaling linearly with γ.

But

Requires post-selection over successful recovery outcomes, reducing total success probability below 1.

Tools

five-qubit permutation-invariant code · probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) · semidefinite programming · Charnes-Cooper transformation

Abstract

Quantum error correcting (QEC) plays a crucial role in protecting quantum information against decoherence and enabling scalable, reliable quantum computing. One of the most realistic and ubiquitous sources of noise affecting quantum hardware today is generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) noise. Conventional, deterministic QEC codes struggle to correct for GAD noise because of their inherent structure, leading to fidelity losses that scale linearly with the damping strength. In this work, we introduce the framework of probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC), that combines the flexibility of approximate QEC with the potential of post-selected recovery, enabling high-fidelity, resource-efficient error correction. We construct a five-qubit permutation-invariant code that, under probabilistic recovery, achieves a fidelity loss quadratic in the damping strength, thus outperforming existing QEC codes. Formulating PAQEC as an optimization problem, we present a numerical technique based on Charnes-Cooper and semidefinite programming to identify the optimal recovery map for any PAQEC code. Our results establish PAQEC as a powerful tool for developing resource-efficient, high-fidelity quantum codes tailored to realistic noise, with promising implications for near-term quantum devices and future fault-tolerant architectures.

item.title: Fermionic quantum error correction is never free
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Code space of any non-trivial [[n,k,dF]] fermionic code with dF≥3 contains zero pure fermionic Gaussian states. Exact unitary codeword preparation via q-mode non-Gaussian gates requires at least g≥⌊(dF−3)/(q−2)⌋+⌈k/q⌉ non-Gaussian gates.

Grade 0.450 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Yifan Tang, Ingo Roth, Philippe Faist, Zi-Wen Liu, Jens Eisert, Zhenhuan Liu

Asks

Can fermionic quantum error correction and error detection be implemented using only free-fermion (Gaussian) operations?

But

Pure fermionic Gaussian states; bounded-weight non-Gaussian unitary circuits acting on n modes; exact and fidelity-bounded codeword preparation.

Tools

Wick's theorem · Knill-Laflamme conditions · fermionic covariance matrices · Schur complement conditioning

Abstract

Fermionic platforms offer compelling architectures for quantum computing, ranging from topologically protected Majorana-based qubits to fermionic cold atoms. To achieve scalability, however, they require quantum error correction. In this work, we prove that any exact and sufficiently accurate approximate fermionic quantum error correction necessarily requires non-Gaussian operations, beyond the free-fermion regime of quadratic dynamics. This is in sharp contrast to the qubit setting, where the efficiently classically simulable stabilizer operations form the standard framework for quantum error correction. Specifically, we show that the logical space of any non-trivial fermionic error-correcting code contains no pure fermionic Gaussian state, utilizing a fundamental incompatibility between fermionic error correction and Wick's theorem. We further show that the required number of bounded-weight non-Gaussian gates for unitary codeword preparation grows at least linearly with both the code distance and the number of encoded modes, revealing an intrinsic resource overhead that increases simultaneously with error-protection strength and logical capacity. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of fermionic Gaussian operations in entanglement distillation, revealing a distinction from their bosonic counterparts. Our results reveal fundamental difficulties for fermionic error correction from the perspectives of both physical implementation and classical simulation, suggesting connections to fermionic phases of matter and state preparation complexity.

item.title: Noise-resilient sequential circuits for generating quantum order
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Unitary sequential circuits with non-Clifford gates prepare 3D symmetry-broken order and 4D (3,1) toric code topological order stably against Pauli noise, with the 4D toric code syndrome cluster size vanishing asymptotically below critical single-qubit error probability pXˆc≈0.013.

Grade 0.448 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Konstantin Gattinger, Julian Boesl, Max McGinley, Michael Knap, Frank Pollmann

Figure

Normalized average maximum syndrome cluster diameter plotted against Pauli error probability pXˆ across multiple linear system sizes L. Below pXˆc≈0.013, relative cluster size scales to zero as L increases, confirming error confinement.

Asks

Can unitary sequential quantum circuits prepare long-range ordered states stably against circuit-level Pauli noise without propagating local errors into nonlocal order-destroying defects?

Before

Standard sequential circuits for 1D GHZ states and 2D toric code wavefunctions are unstable to Pauli noise at any non-zero error rate due to gate-propagated errors.

But

Requires spatial dimension D≥3 for purely unitary stabilization (or D≥2 with active measurement and classical feedback); stabilizer syndromes must form closed manifolds of dimension d≥2.

Tools

sequential unitary circuits · majority-vote and Toom's rule gate updates · cellular automaton simulations · higher-dimensional stabilizer syndrome analysis

Abstract

Sequential circuits provide an optimal linear-depth route to unitarily preparing long-range ordered quantum states, but circuit-level noise can be far more damaging than noise applied after preparation: local errors may be propagated by subsequent gates into nonlocal defects that destroy the target order. In this work, we present classes of unitary sequential circuits that prepare certain non-trivial orders in the presence of Pauli noise. Our constructions exploit the spatial structure of the syndromes of the target state, which in certain cases allows us to systematically suppress the propagation of errors using strictly local gates. The strategy can be applied both to symmetry-breaking order, for which we present a 3D example, and to topological order, which we showcase on a 4D version of the toric code. We also highlight how this stability against errors necessitates non-Clifford gates, and how measurement-feedback loops can be used to stabilize lower-dimensional states as well.

item.title: WISER: Systematic Design-Space Exploration of Fault-Tolerant Global Control Trapped-Ions
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Optimal SAT compilation improves globally controlled WISE logical clock speed from 1.94 Hz to 4.28 Hz for a distance-7 surface code, but remains roughly 3× slower than local QCCD control at 12.8 Hz.

Grade 0.440 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms” · Scott Jones, Song-qing-hao Yang, Prakash Murali

Figure

Logical error rate (horizontal axis) versus logical clock speed (vertical axis) across pessimistic, current, and optimistic technology tiers at fixed hardware parameters. Only bivariate-bicycle distance-4 under the optimistic tier achieves <10−8 error while staying below the 1 W per logical qubit power limit.

Asks

Is the performance gap between globally multiplexed trapped-ion control and standard QCCD an intrinsic architectural bottleneck or an artifact of suboptimal compilation and hardware choices?

Before

Heuristic compilation on WISE achieved 1.94 Hz clock speed and 3.3×10−6 logical error rate (Jones and Murali 2026), compared to 12.8 Hz on QCCD.

But

Evaluated on logical memory benchmarking rather than full computation; assumes optimistic physical noise reductions and ignores boundary-qubit routing from lattice surgery.

Tools

WISER cross-layer co-design framework · SAT-based odd-even routing compiler · physics-grounded ion noise and heating model · Stim circuit-level simulations

Abstract

Trapped-ion quantum computers are a leading candidate for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing, but conventional Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (QCCD) architectures face severe wiring and power constraints as systems scale. The recently proposed WISE promise orders-of-magnitude reductions in wiring complexity but fundamentally alter the hardware--software interface, making it unclear whether such restrictive architectures can feasibly execute quantum error correction (QEC) and eventually support fault-tolerant workloads. We present WISER, a cross-layer architectural design-space exploration framework for globally controlled trapped-ion systems, to determine whether WISE can support early FTQC, and what hardware/compiler/QEC choices are needed. WISER combines novel WISE-specific compilation, noise modelling, and simulation and integrated them into a unified framework. WISER provides comparative lower-bound estimates of logical clock speed and logical error rate, rather than absolute hardware prediction, enabling us to identify viable operating regions while ruling out infeasible ones. To our knowledge, it is the first systematic design space exploration study targeted at WISE and scalable architectures beyond QCCD. Using WISER, we identify a narrow feasible design space requiring two-ion traps, moderate control multiplexing, aggressive recooling, and high-rate bivariate-bicycle codes. Even under ∼10× improvements in physical errors, the lower-bound cycle time to achieve < 10⁻⁸ logical error is ≈100 ms, which is 3× slower than local control. These results expose a fundamental trade-off between wiring scalability and logical throughput, suggesting that practical early fault-tolerant operation requires complementary > 10× physical error rate reductions along with substantial > 100× reduction in fault-tolerant circuit-depth.

item.title: NAQsim: Full-Stack Architecture Simulation Framework for Fast and Space-Efficient Neutral Atom Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Patch rotations cause 55.3% to 77.6% of execution time in transversal neutral-atom FTQC. The D3-ROT architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding an average 2.27× speedup (up to 2.57×) at 22.4% average footprint overhead.

Grade 0.428 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Yosuke Ueno, Shinichi Sunami, Toshihide Hinokuma, Yasunari Suzuki, Akihisa Goban, Hayata Yamasaki, Teruo Tanimoto, Ilkwon Byun

Figure

Per-layer latency breakdown (bars, left axis) and logical error rate (line, right axis) across six routing and patch-rotation architectures, showing D3-ROT minimizing latency without sacrificing error rates.

Asks

How can full-stack co-optimization across compiler, control hardware, and qubit plane reduce logical operation latency in transversal neutral-atom FTQC architectures?

Before

Patch rotations executed via space-efficient reflection on baseline transversal surface-code architectures.

But

Evaluated via classical CPU simulation across 8 FTQC benchmark circuits (QPE and FTCircuitBench) using rotated transversal surface codes.

Tools

NAQsim architecture simulation framework · SLM laser toggling with AOD atom holding · heterogeneous qubit-plane rotation patches · rotation distribution compiler pass

Code. https://github.com/naqsim/naqsim

Abstract

Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

item.arxave:abstract: Technological advances in neutral-atom platforms have opened a new path toward designing efficient protocols for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, each physical operation is still orders of magnitude slower than on other platforms, such as superconducting qubits. Therefore, architects must identify fast and efficient FTQC architectures, which require reliable modeling tools to explore various design choices across the software, classical hardware, and quantum device stacks of neutral-atom platforms. In this paper, we propose NAQsim, an open-source simulation framework for neutral-atom FTQC architectures based on transversal gates. As its key feature, NAQsim enables detailed full-stack architecture evaluation that opens opportunities to explore previously overlooked performance bottlenecks. As a first use case for NAQsim, we identify one such bottleneck, patch rotations, perform full-stack co-optimization, and finally derive a near-rotation-free architecture (D3-ROT). For practical FTQC benchmark workloads, D3-ROT achieves a 2.27x speedup from this single bottleneck alone, with minimal footprint overhead. These results point to a much broader space of full-stack optimizations that NAQsim makes accessible for transversal surface-code architectures and beyond.

item.title: CUDA-Q Logical: Retargetable Compilation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — CUDA-Q Logical provides an MLIR-based, retargetable compiler pipeline that lowers logical quantum programs through five explicit semantic profiles (P0 to P4), directly deriving resource estimates, detector error models, and physical execution schedules from compiler artifacts while preserving provenance.

Grade 0.427 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms” · Alexander McCaskey, Justin Lietz, Adam Holmes, Kohei Nakaji, Vadym Kliuchnikov, Yifan Hong, Amalee Wilson, Andres Paz, Bettina Heim, Bruno Schmitt, Krysta M. Svore

Figure

Progression of compiler lowering across five semantic profiles from P0 logical intent down to P4 real-time control, illustrating typed boundaries for research components and analysis passes.

Asks

How can fault-tolerant quantum compilation unify target-independent logical intent, heterogeneous QEC encodings, physical scheduling, and real-time control to provide verifiable, reproducible resource estimates and cross-architecture comparisons?

But

Deterministic and single-shot behavior only; rejects retry averaging, stochastic queues, dynamic routing, packetization, and runtime boundary-changing surgery in compact models.

Tools

MLIR progressive lowering pipeline · CUDA-Q platform · Spacetime plan and transport modeling · Extended detector error models (EDEM) · qLDPC code surgery templates

Abstract

Realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing requires mapping logical programs to heterogeneous quantum error correction (QEC) codes and diverse fault-tolerant execution models, scheduling physical resources, and coupling to real-time classical control and feedback. Specialized tools exist for each step but rely on manual composition and translation that discard assumptions and provenance, separating resource estimates from the compiler artifacts they describe, and making it difficult to validate correctness, compare architectures, or attribute costs to specific design choices. We present CUDA-Q Logical, an extensible compiler infrastructure for retargetable fault-tolerant compilation, analysis, and execution. Interoperable with CUDA-Q and other mainstream front-ends, CUDA-Q Logical progressively lowers target-independent logical programs through a constrained logical virtual machine, QEC microcode, physical gate schedules, and real-time control plans, with each layer preserving semantics and provenance, while verifying composition and resource constraints. By deriving every resource estimate directly from compiler artifacts, the framework unifies compilation and resource analysis, enabling successively refined estimates and principled cross-architecture comparison while permitting QEC codes, execution models, decoders, and hardware architectures to be introduced as modular extensions. Across workloads ranging from application-architecture studies to qLDPC surgery and detector-error-model composition, we show that schedule-derived estimates reconcile with established independent models. Crucially, this compiler-visible structure exposes cost drivers hidden by aggregate analytical formulas, carries QEC artifacts intact into simulation, and demonstrates a complete compilation pipeline for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: A Modular, Topology-Aware Software Stack for Entanglement-Based Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by 17.7±1.3% and 17.9±1.5% relative to FIFO.

Grade 0.411 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Luke Andreesen, Shobhit Gupta, Sean Sullivan, Manish Kumar Singh

Figure

EPR-pair consumption (y-axis) for 18-qubit QFT and 64-qubit Adder circuits on a 2-QPU network under all-to-all versus nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity (x-axis) across three partitioning strategies.

Asks

How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?

Before

Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.

But

NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.

Tools

OpenQASM compiler toolchain · Discrete-event stochastic scheduler · Quantum Network Constructor (QNC) · Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners · Cat-Entangler and Cat-Disentangler teleportation protocols

Code. https://github.com/memQGit/dqc

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) seeks to scale beyond the limits of monolithic processors by interconnecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through entanglement-based links. Realizing this vision requires the co-design of hardware and software across the domains of quantum networking, compilation, and scheduling, yet existing tools remain fragmented between monolithic circuit compilers and long-distance quantum network simulators. We present an open-source, topology-informed framework for the compilation and scheduling of distributed quantum programs. Given an input circuit and a description of the target network, the framework partitions and reconstructs the circuit into a distributed program that respects the specified inter- and intra-QPU topology, covers cross-QPU operations through gate and state teleportation, and schedules the result under either deterministic or stochastic entanglement-generation models. By accepting and emitting standard OpenQASM, the framework interoperates with existing monolithic toolchains, and its standardized module interfaces allow partitioning and scheduling strategies to be interchanged and benchmarked. Using this framework, we show that the best-performing compilation strategy varies across the tested circuits and network configurations, and that both network topology and intra-QPU connectivity substantially affect the entanglement cost of execution. These findings underscore the need for a co-design approach to distributed quantum computing, which our framework is designed to support.
